# A common surface-area submeasure survives Minkowski averaging

Let d>=2. For a convex body K in R^d, S_K denotes its surface-area
measure on S^(d-1): boundary H_(d-1) pushed forward by the almost
everywhere uniquely defined outer unit normal. Thus for a polytope the
atom at a facet normal is precisely that facet's (d-1)-volume.

**Theorem.** If A,B are convex bodies and nu is a finite nonnegative
Borel measure with nu<=S_A and nu<=S_B, then, for every 0<=t<=1,

    S_((1-t)A+tB) >= nu.                                  (1)

In particular, with M=(A+B)/2,

    S_M >= S_A wedge S_B,                                 (2)

where the wedge has density min(dS_A/dsigma,dS_B/dsigma) relative to
sigma=S_A+S_B. This includes arbitrary singular continuous parts, atoms,
and mixtures of singular and absolutely continuous parts. No smoothness
or strict convexity is required.

The proof uses a coupled atomic approximation of the THREE measures
nu, S_A-nu, S_B-nu. It never takes a weak limit of independently formed
wedges, an operation which would not justify (2).

## 1. Vector-preserving atomic approximation

Let eta be any finite nonnegative measure on the sphere. For a finite
Borel partition P_delta into cells of Euclidean diameter at most delta<1,
write

    v_E(eta)=integral_E u d eta(u),
    eta_delta=sum_(E:eta(E)>0) |v_E(eta)| delta_(v_E(eta)/|v_E(eta)|).
                                                               (3)

Every listed vector is nonzero. Indeed, choose u_E in E; then
u_E.u>=1-delta^2/2 throughout E, whence

 (1-delta^2/2)eta(E)<=|v_E(eta)|<=eta(E).                  (4)

The first vector moment is preserved EXACTLY:

    integral u d eta_delta(u)=integral u d eta(u).        (5)

Moreover eta_delta converges weakly to eta as delta tends to zero.
To verify this directly, the normalized vector in (3) lies within
2delta of u_E: its unnormalized average lies within delta, and
normalization moves it by at most delta. Thus a continuous test varies
by at most its modulus of continuity at 3delta between the atom and
points in E. The mass discrepancy is at most delta^2 eta(E)/2 by (4).
Summing gives convergence for every continuous test. Zero cells are
omitted; the zero measure is approximated by the zero measure.

This operation is NOT asserted to be additive in eta. We apply it
separately to fixed positive components and add the resulting atoms.
Preservation of (5) is what makes that construction legitimate.

## 2. Coupled polytope approximation with a retained common measure

Set alpha=S_A-nu and beta=S_B-nu. On one sequence of partitions with
diameter tending to zero, form nu_N, alpha_N, beta_N by (3), and put

    mu_N^A=nu_N+alpha_N,   mu_N^B=nu_N+beta_N.             (6)

These finite atomic measures converge weakly to S_A,S_B respectively,
share the exact common submeasure nu_N, and have first vector moment
zero. The latter follows from (5) and the equilibrium identity
integral u dS_K(u)=0.

For all sufficiently large N, neither full measure in (6) is concentrated
on a great subsphere. Here is a useful explicit justification. For any
full-dimensional convex body K,

    q_K(v)=integral |u.v| dS_K(u)>0  for every |v|=1.

The continuous function q_K has a positive minimum on the sphere;
equivalently, its area measure is not concentrated on a great subsphere.
Weak convergence and the uniformly bounded total masses imply uniform
convergence of the displayed integrals as functions of v: use a finite
net and the bound ||u.v|-|u.w||<=|v-w|. The approximants therefore have
the same positive lower bound up to a factor two. This rules out a great
subsphere. Equilibrium then also rules out concentration on a closed
hemisphere unless the measure is on its bounding great subsphere.

The classical discrete Minkowski existence theorem gives convex polytopes
A_N,B_N with area measures exactly (6), unique up to translation. The
standard theorem needed here says that a finite nonzero spherical
measure is an area measure precisely when it has equilibrium and is not
concentrated on a great subsphere; finite support gives a polytope.

For a primary mathematical statement of these standard hypotheses and
uniqueness, see the introduction of R. Schneider,
[Minkowski type theorems for convex sets in cones](https://home.mathematik.uni-freiburg.de/rschnei/Minkowski.cones.pdf),
which refers to the classical compact-body theorem before addressing
cones. Only that classical theorem is used here.

After suitable translations and passage to a subsequence,

    A_N -> A',   B_N -> B'                               (7)

in Hausdorff distance, where A',B' are translates of A,B. For completeness
the compactness and noncollapse required for this familiar Minkowski
stability assertion are verified next, rather than inferred from weak
convergence alone.

## 3. The required inverse continuity, with no escaping shapes

Suppose S_(K_N) tends weakly to S_K for a full-dimensional convex body K.
The preceding finite-net argument and the Cauchy projection formula give
constants 0<c<C<infinity, independent of large N and unit v, such that

    c<=vol_(d-1)(K_N projected to v-perp)<=C.              (8)

Choose a John ellipsoid E_N of K_N and translate its center to zero.
John's theorem gives E_N subset K_N subset d E_N. Let its positive
semiaxes be a_1,...,a_d and put p=product a_i. Projection in its i-th
principal direction has volume omega_(d-1) p/a_i. From (8) and the two
containments,

    c/(d^(d-1)omega_(d-1)) <= p/a_i <= C/omega_(d-1).      (9)

Multiplying (9) over i bounds p^(d-1) above and away from zero. Using
(9) again bounds EVERY a_i above and away from zero. Thus the translated
bodies lie in one fixed ball and contain another fixed positive ball.
Blaschke compactness gives a Hausdorff convergent subsequence with a
full-dimensional limit K'. Surface-area measures are weakly continuous
under this convergence, so S_(K')=S_K. Minkowski uniqueness gives K' a
translate of K. Applying this argument successively to A_N and B_N
proves (7) on a common subsequence.

The standard Cauchy identity used in (8) is

 vol_(d-1)(K projected to v-perp)=(1/2)integral |u.v| dS_K(u).

It holds without symmetry; for a polytope it follows by projecting its
facets, with almost every projected interior point covered once from
each side. General bodies follow by polytope approximation. Weak
continuity of area measures is likewise standard: their integrals against
support functions are d times mixed volumes, which are Hausdorff
continuous. Differences of support functions are dense in continuous
spherical functions (smooth functions become support functions after
adding a sufficiently large constant), yielding weak continuity.
See also D. Hug and R. Schneider,
[Hölder continuity for support measures of convex bodies](https://arxiv.org/abs/1501.06214),
for a stronger quantitative statement. These are ordinary convex-geometry
facts, not a mixed-integer or depth theorem.

## 4. Facet Brunn--Minkowski and the limit

Let M_N=(1-t)A_N+tB_N. At every atom u of nu_N, both exposed faces
A_N(u),B_N(u) are facets, with respective areas at least nu_N({u}).
The exact exposed-face identity is

    M_N(u)=(1-t)A_N(u)+tB_N(u).

Translate the two parallel faces into the same (d-1)-dimensional vector
space. Brunn--Minkowski there gives

 S_(M_N)({u})^(1/(d-1))
   >=(1-t)S_(A_N)({u})^(1/(d-1))
       +t S_(B_N)({u})^(1/(d-1))
   >=nu_N({u})^(1/(d-1)).                                (10)

Any coincident atoms from the separate components in (6) simply add to
the relevant face area; (10) is unchanged. At normals not charged by
nu_N the desired inequality is vacuous. Hence

    S_(M_N)>=nu_N                                        (11)

as finite measures, not merely after testing a particular cap or normal.
The cases t=0 or t=1 are also immediate from (6).

By (7), M_N tends to a translate of (1-t)A+tB. Area measures are
translation invariant and weakly continuous. Test (11) against any
nonnegative continuous function, then pass to the limit using nu_N->nu.
The resulting inequality characterizes domination of finite Borel
measures on the compact sphere and proves (1). Choosing the wedge gives
(2). This finishes the singular case without smoothing either body.

## 5. Weighted common-measure extension

The same proof gives a slightly more general exact statement. Let K_j
be finitely many convex bodies, lambda_j>=0 with sum lambda_j=1, and
assume S_(K_j)>=a_j nu for fixed a_j>=0. Then

 S_(sum_j lambda_j K_j)
   >=[sum_j lambda_j a_j^(1/(d-1))]^(d-1) nu.             (12)

Indeed approximate the common component nu ONCE, and each residual
S_(K_j)-a_j nu separately. The full atomic measures still have exact
equilibrium. At each common atom apply (d-1)-dimensional BM to the exposed
faces, retaining a zero-area face if a_j=0. If the right side of (12)
is positive, at least one positively weighted face has positive area;
the usual BM inequality includes the remaining nonempty lower-dimensional
faces. If its coefficient is zero the conclusion is trivial. The same
simultaneous compactness and weak-limit argument applies.

The factor one in (1) is sharp: A=B and nu=S_A give equality. This theorem
is a measure statement on normals. It does not allocate physical boundary
points within an exposed face, supply cap losses, or prove compatibility
of a prescribed mixed-fiber erosion. Those remain separate requirements
in any OC application.

## 6. Full measure-level Brunn--Minkowski root inequality

The weighted common-measure form yields a stronger conclusion without
any further approximation of convex bodies. Put sigma=S_A+S_B and choose
Radon--Nikodym densities f=dS_A/dsigma and g=dS_B/dsigma, with f+g=1
almost everywhere. Then

 S_((1-t)A+tB)
   >=[(1-t) f^(1/(d-1))+t g^(1/(d-1))]^(d-1) sigma.       (13)

Here is the measure-theoretic step in full. For a positive integer N,
partition the sphere, outside a sigma-null set, by the finitely many
values of (floor(Nf),floor(Ng)). On a cell E having lower values
a=floor(Nf)/N and b=floor(Ng)/N, the measures S_A,S_B dominate
a sigma|E and b sigma|E respectively. Apply (12) with nu=sigma|E.
Since these cells are disjoint, the resulting measure inequalities add:
for a Borel set D sum the bound on D intersect E. This gives (13) with
f,g replaced by their lower step approximants. They approach f,g uniformly
to within 1/N. The scalar function
((1-t)a^(1/(d-1))+t b^(1/(d-1)))^(d-1) is uniformly continuous on the
compact square [0,1]^2. Integration against finite sigma and passage to
the limit therefore prove (13) on every Borel D. Null sets do not matter.

The same argument, with a finite product partition of the density ranges,
works for any finite weighted Minkowski sum in (12). The limiting density
is the corresponding weighted (d-1)-root sum. Homothetic bodies attain
equality in (13). In d=2 it reduces to the familiar exact linearity of
the first surface-area measure under Minkowski addition; in higher
dimensions additional positive measure may be present where the original
two area measures both vanish.
